title: You Have No Horses to Give Him, and No Money
intro: Al-Mutanabbi addressed this poem to Abu Shuja' Fatik in Egypt in 348 AH (959–960 CE). Al-Wahidi quotes Ibn Jinni’s report that Fatik once sent the poet gifts worth a thousand dinars at a stroke. Trying to answer such a gift, the poet likens himself to good ground where rain comes up in flower. The last verse returns to what a poem can give its subject, a second life in other people’s memory.

translation: You have no horses to give him, and no money.
Let speech come to your aid if means will not.
1.sharh: The opening “you” is the poet addressing himself. Until the addressee becomes clear, it almost sounds as though he is telling his wealthy patron that he owns nothing. Speech offers a currency he really can spend.

translation: Repay the emir whose bounty comes by surprise,
without a word. Other men’s gifts are promises.
2.sharh: The emir gets the gift there before any promise has been made. Words are worthless in the mouths of donors who do nothing, yet the poet has just staked his whole return gift on the worth of his words.

translation: A benefactor may find his kindness repaid
even by a shy, indolent maiden of the camp.
3.sharh: The verb and the favour come first in Arabic, with the unlikely giver delayed to the second half. A reserved young woman in the camp can find a way to acknowledge kindness. It leaves the poet little excuse for silence.

translation: Though tight hobbles keep me from showing
how I run, I can still neigh in them.
4.sharh: The absent gift horse reappears as a figure for the speaker. A hobble can keep a good horse from demonstrating its paces without taking away its voice. Al-Wahidi also hears the limits of openly backing Fatik at Kafur’s court.

translation: I do not thank him because the money cheered me.
Plenty and little are all one to me.
5.sharh: He disclaims dependence on the size of his purse. That makes the thanks due even if the windfall makes no difference to his standard of living. The argument has moved from need to obligation.

translation: But it seemed ugly to be treated so generously
and be miserly ourselves in paying what we owe.
6.sharh: The person who received everything can still be the miser in the exchange. Praise is something he has it in his power to withhold. The shift from “I” to “we” invites his listeners to feel the awkwardness too.

translation: I was the growing ground of an upland meadow
visited at dawn by rain that pours on no salt waste.
7.sharh: The gift is rain and this poem is what grows where it falls. The speaker boasts quietly of his own fertility as a recipient while describing his patron’s discrimination as a giver.

translation: The place where this rain falls shows onlookers
how little ordinary rains know of what they water.
8.sharh: Ordinary rain has no way to choose its ground. Fatik has found a recipient who can turn a gift into lasting verse. The success of the comparison gives the poet grounds for surpassing it.

translation: Only a quick-witted lord can attain glory,
one who does time and again what other lords find hard.
9.sharh: The test is set among people who can already claim to be lords. In Arabic the last word describes someone who does a thing repeatedly. Another chief’s exceptional effort is this man’s familiar work.

translation: He inherited nothing. His right hand loses count of its gifts.
He begs from no one and wins his wealth by the sword.
10.sharh: Al-Wahidi says Fatik’s father was so generous that he left him nothing. Fatik gives away wealth he has won at his own risk, and his giving hand has long since lost count.

translation: Time spoke to him and made him understand.
Time has sharp words for the man who hoards.
11.sharh: Time’s way of speaking is to change who owns things. The listener who understands this can turn a temporary possession into an enduring reputation before it is taken from him.

translation: When the spear quivers in his palm it knows
that horses and champions will suffer for it.
12.sharh: The weapon is personified at the instant its bearer takes hold of it. The slightest tremor tells it what sort of hand it is in and what will happen to both mounts and riders.

translation: Like Fatik, though that word “like” diminishes him.
I said “like the sun”, and the sun has no peer.
13.sharh: “Like Fatik” finally supplies a name for the kind of lord the poet set out to define. He then catches himself in the act of comparison. There is no second sun with which to complete a strict likeness.

translation: He leads lions his own claws have fed
on their likes among his foes since they were cubs.
14.sharh: The enemy must be formidable to make fit prey for these lions. The “cubs” add a history to the picture. What looks like native ferocity in the troops is also the result of their commander’s training.

translation: He kills the sword inside the man it kills.
Swords, like men, have their appointed end.
15.sharh: The weapon breaks inside the person it strikes. By counting the blade as a second casualty the poet can grant swords something otherwise reserved for the living, the day fixed for their death.

translation: Dread of him raids the raiders in his stead,
while his camels range unguarded at the earth’s far ends.
16.sharh: The herds are far from home and have no one to look after them. The remembered name of their owner reaches them all the same, meeting the raider before he can even begin his raid.

translation: His is whatever game his spearheads choose,
wild ass, cock ostrich, wild cow or trailing-tailed bull.
17.sharh: The list is a hunter’s inventory. Two of the animals are named by a feature one might pick out at a distance, the cow’s receding nose and the bull’s trailing tail. To choose any one of them is to have it.

translation: At his door the guests have whatever they fancy.
All their hours are as pleasant as late afternoon.
18.sharh: Late afternoon brought a break from the heat and a welcome breeze. His guests enjoy that hour’s comforts at every time of day, beginning at the open ground immediately outside his house.

translation: If they had a taste for their host’s own flesh,
pieces and whole joints of him would hurry to their bowls.
19.sharh: The hypothetical appetite would consume hospitality’s very source. Yet the kitchen detail is exact, down to the wooden serving bowls and the difference between small cuts and joints. The gruesome impossibility is served promptly.

translation: He knows no bereavement over wealth or children
except when departure drives his guests away.
20.sharh: A departure from the table is made the measure of losses a household would ordinarily count far more serious. Even the guests seem reluctant, since the compulsion to travel has to drive them out.

translation: What remains of their drink quenches the earth’s thirst,
pure milk of the milch camels and clear, easy-flowing wine.
21.sharh: The earth drinks after the guests have finished. Ibn Jinni, as quoted by al-Wahidi, takes the discarded remainder to mean that each new arrival receives a fresh supply. The clear second drink is wine in the commentaries.

translation: His blades serve the hours fresh-drawn blood,
as though the hours were callers or travellers returning home.
22.sharh: Time keeps arriving like a succession of travellers, each entitled to fresh meat. Ibn Jinni also understands blood shed in combat. Both senses are in play when the poet names whose blood runs in the next verse.

translation: Lives flow mingled all around him,
those of foes, of sheep and of camels.
23.sharh: The word for lives can mean the blood in which life resides. Once it flows, the distinction between the combatant’s victim and the host’s livestock disappears to the eye. The list at the end restores it.

translation: Distance cannot deny distant people his gifts.
Even little children can reach what he gives.
24.sharh: Two obstacles are removed, geography and the ability to petition. Arabic makes the already small children smaller with a diminutive. Even someone unable to make the trip can be reached by the gift.

translation: His edge is keenest against his peers in either army
when bright swords find their way and brown spears go astray.
25.sharh: Weapons are recognisable from their colours alone. The commentary attributed to al-Ukbari sees the armies closing so tightly that long lances cannot manoeuvre. The man with the sure sword proves himself at that distance.

translation: Test him and he proves worth many times his looks.
Among men are both real water and mirage.
26.sharh: The traveller has to reach the gleam on the horizon before he knows whether he can drink. The same test of approach and experience distinguishes men whose outward appearance promises the same thing.

translation: An envier may call him Madman
when weapons mingle. Some good sense can lame a horse.
27.sharh: Fatik really carried the nickname “Madman”. The defence turns on the kinship in sound between reason and a complaint that cripples an animal’s legs. There are moments when being sensible can leave a rider stranded.

translation: He flings his horses at an army. He and they
must cleave it, though the army be mountains.
28.sharh: The commander cannot send his cavalry ahead and stay behind, since the syntax binds him and his horses to the same necessity. The mountain comparison gives the enemy every advantage in solidity.

translation: Once his claws have taken hold of the foe,
they cannot have both a lion and a mild temper.
29.sharh: To an opponent actually caught in his claws, asking for leniency is as unreasonable as expecting a lion to deliberate. The nickname in verse 27 is being answered from the enemy’s point of view.

translation: They dread in him a fate whose blows come openly,
while the blows of ordinary fate spring from hiding.
30.sharh: The turns of fortune usually get the better of their victims by surprise. Fatik can produce the same terror in full view. That changes the comparison from a measure of power into a judgement on how he uses it.

translation: Advancing won him the highest honour.
What did they win by avoiding what he dared?
31.sharh: The reward for advancing has a name and occupies the whole first half. The cautious men get a space in which to name their own reward. The question leaves that space pointedly empty.

translation: When kings put on their jewels, his ornaments
are an Indian blade and a quivering, solid-jointed spear.
32.sharh: Court dress and battle gear are being laid out side by side. The spear has strength where its joints meet and spring along its length, qualities that make it a more telling ornament for him than jewels.

translation: Abu Shuja', father of every brave man,
a terror reared by the terrors of battle.
33.sharh: Abu Shuja' can be heard as “father of a brave man”. Praise expands a conventional name into fatherhood of the whole company of the brave, then imagines battle itself as the parent that brought him up.

translation: He owns praise so completely that no boaster
has an h, an m or a d of praise to claim.
34.sharh: The Arabic stem for praise consists of the three consonants h, m and d. Fatik has taken title to each individual letter as well as to the thing the word names. A rival cannot even spell out a claim.

translation: He wears layer upon layer of shirts of praise,
though one shirt of supple mail has served him well.
35.sharh: Praise, newly taken apart into letters, is woven back together as protective clothing. His reputation has many layers of defence. For his person under attack he asks for only a single coat.

translation: How could I hide the good you have done me,
when you have flooded me with gifts, generous giver?
36.sharh: The poet turns to Fatik in person. Arabic brings the gift and the name it earns the giver almost into a single sound. His thanks could hardly conceal so recognisable a source.

translation: You found a subtle way to show me kindness and honour.
A noble man takes pains to find a way to greatness.
37.sharh: The thought that went into arranging the gift counts as another gift. Al-Wahidi connects this discretion with the political delicacy of showing favour to the poet in Egypt. Ingenuity serves an honourable end here.

translation: And so word of you travels everywhere,
and the stars themselves have hopes of your two hands.
38.sharh: Discretion in the act of giving has done nothing to keep its news at home. After the stories have ranged the world, expectation travels vertically as well. Even the stars look towards the giver’s hands.

translation: My praise grew long because its wearer stands tall.
Praise fitted to a dwarf is short itself.
39.sharh: The length of the panegyric, which the listener has now felt, is the measure taken for its garment. Shortness in the example belongs first to the model, then to the verse cut to fit him.

translation: Though you are above strutting among men,
your standing struts among the ranks of others.
40.sharh: A man can refuse to parade his importance and still tower over his fellows. To let both things be seen at once, the poet gives rank a gait and leaves its owner quietly where he is.

translation: Your own soul seems unwilling to have you for its companion
unless you outgive even the open-handed.
41.sharh: His own soul acts like a demanding companion who could leave an unworthy man. It will not be satisfied by ordinary generosity. Its measure is what he can do beyond the performance of another proven giver.

translation: Nor will it think you guard its heart’s blood well
unless you spend it freely in the hour of fear.
42.sharh: The pledge to guard his soul reverses the usual terms of safekeeping. He must be ready to spend the life entrusted to him. Courage is thus brought under the same word for expenditure as generosity.

translation: Without hardship, everyone would be a lord.
Giving brings poverty, and boldness gets men killed.
43.sharh: The two costs have been prepared in the preceding verses. Money can disappear from giving and life from stepping forward. The very things a person might hope to enjoy as a lord are the things put at risk in getting there.

translation: A man can reach only as far as his strength allows.
Not every saddle-bearer is a swift she-camel.
44.sharh: From a distance all the camels in a caravan do the same job and carry the same equipment. The limits of their powers tell only on the road. The image gives that distinction back to the people being compared.

translation: We live in a time when merely refraining from harm
counts as kindness and decency in most people.
45.sharh: The ordinary scale of expectation has sunk so low that leaving somebody unharmed earns thanks. Against that background, the unasked-for gift which began the poem becomes exceptional once more.

translation: A man’s good name is his second life. He needs
only what sustains him. Everything beyond that keeps him busy.
46.sharh: Fatik’s gifts sustain the poet while he lives. The poet can give his patron something that outlasts the gifts, a name that people will keep speaking.

1.2.1.head: أَسعَدَ
1.2.1.meaning: Come to someone’s aid, here by helping the speaker repay a favour.

2.1.4.head: نُعمى
2.1.4.meaning: Bounty or a particular act of kindness.

2.1.5.head: فاجِئَة
2.1.5.meaning: Arriving unexpectedly, before a request or a promise.

3.1.4.head: مولٍ
3.1.4.meaning: The person who bestows a benefit.

3.2.5.head: مِكسال
3.2.5.meaning: Slow to stir or act, describing the young woman.

4.1.4.head: شُكل
4.1.4.meaning: Hobbles, bindings put on a horse’s legs to prevent it running off.

5.2.1.head: سِيّان
5.2.1.meaning: Equal, of two things of the same weight or worth.

6.2.4.head: بُخّال
6.2.4.meaning: Misers, here people who begrudge even an acknowledgement.

7.1.3-4.head: رَوض الحَزن
7.1.3-4.meaning: “Meadows of the upland”, growing ground on high, rough terrain.

7.2.3.head: سِباخ
7.2.3.meaning: Salt flats, ground in which little grows.

8.1.3.head: نُظّار
8.1.3.meaning: Onlookers able to see what the gift produces.

9.2.5.head: فَعّال
9.2.5.meaning: Habitually accomplishing something, an intensive form.

10.2.5.head: سَأّال
10.2.5.meaning: Someone habitually asking other people for money.

11.2.4.head: إِمساك
11.2.4.meaning: Holding back money from use or from a petitioner.

11.2.5.head: عَذّال
11.2.5.meaning: An insistent reprover, here time itself.

12.1.2.head: قَناة
12.1.2.meaning: A lance, by reference to its long shaft.

12.1.5.head: راحَة
12.1.5.meaning: The palm of the hand that grips the spear.

13.1.1.head: فاتِك
13.1.1.meaning: Fatik, the Egyptian commander Abu Shuja', nicknamed the Madman.

13.1.3.head: الكاف
13.1.3.meaning: Kaf, the prefixed Arabic word for “like” in both comparisons.

14.1.4.head: بُرثُن
14.1.4.meaning: The claws or paw of a beast of prey.

14.2.5.head: شِبل
14.2.5.meaning: Lion cubs, here the men early in their training.

15.2.4.head: أَجَل
15.2.4.meaning: Appointed limits of a life, here ascribed to swords.

16.2.4.head: أَهمال
16.2.4.meaning: Camels allowed to range with no herdsman.

17.2.1.head: عَير
17.2.1.meaning: A wild ass, particularly the male.

17.2.3.head: خَنساء
17.2.3.meaning: A wild cow named for its short or receding nose.

17.2.4.head: ذَيّال
17.2.4.meaning: A wild bull named for the tail trailing behind it.

18.1.3.head: مُشَهّاة
18.1.3.meaning: Catered for according to each guest’s own wishes.

18.1.4.head: عَقوَة
18.1.4.meaning: The open space around a house or immediately outside its door.

18.2.5.head: أَصيل
18.2.5.meaning: The late afternoons, when the heat eases.

19.1.4.head: قارٍ
19.1.4.meaning: The host who supplies a guest’s meal.

19.2.1.head: خَرادِل
19.2.1.meaning: Small cuts of meat. A form with dh in place of d is also transmitted.

19.2.4.meaning: Shiza, a wood used for serving bowls, hence the bowls themselves.

19.2.5.head: وِصل
19.2.5.meaning: Whole limbs or joints of meat.

20.1.3.head: رُزء
20.1.3.meaning: Bereavement or a grievous loss of property.

21.1.2.meaning: Thirst, attributed to the ground that receives the leftovers.

21.2.1-2.head: مَحض اللِّقاح
21.2.1-2.meaning: “The pure milk of the milch camels”, undiluted with water.

21.2.5.head: سَلسال
21.2.5.meaning: Easy to swallow, smooth-flowing of drink.

22.1.1.head: قَرى
22.1.1.meaning: To serve a guest a meal, here an office assigned to the blades.

23.1.2.head: نَفس
23.1.2.meaning: Lives or souls, also the life-blood flowing from a wound.

23.2.4.head: آبال
23.2.4.meaning: Herds of camels, an enlarged plural of the collective noun.

24.2.4.head: أُطَيفال
24.2.4.meaning: Tiny children, a diminutive applied to the plural.

25.1.5.head: ظُبَة
25.1.5.meaning: The cutting edge of a sword.

25.2.1.head: البيض
25.2.1.meaning: “The white ones”, swords identified by their bright metal blades.

26.2.5.head: آل
26.2.5.meaning: A mirage that looks like water from a distance.

27.2.5.head: عُقّال
27.2.5.meaning: A disorder of an animal’s legs that hinders its gait. It sounds like the Arabic word for reason.

28.2.6.head: أَجبال
28.2.6.meaning: Mountains, an older plural used of the enemy’s solidity.

29.2.2.head: اِجتَمَعَ
29.2.2.meaning: To occur together. The recitation points to tajtami' with initial t. The commentaries and the recording’s text card have yajtami', agreeing with the two masculine nouns, “forbearance” and “lion”.

30.1.4.head: صَرف
30.1.4.meaning: A turn or stroke of fortune.

31.2.3.head: تَوَقٍّ
31.2.3.meaning: Taking precautions against a danger. The same risk that the others avoided is the one Fatik advanced to meet.

32.2.2-3.head: أَصَمّ الكَعب
32.2.2-3.meaning: “Solid at the joints”, said of a strong spear shaft. Al-Wahidi has this reading with sad.

32.2.4.head: عَسّال
32.2.4.meaning: Quivering or flexing in its bearer’s hand.

34.2.3.head: حاء
34.2.3.meaning: Ha, the first of the three root letters in hamd, “praise”.

35.1.3.head: سِربال
35.1.3.meaning: Garments or coats, here layers of protection for a good name.

36.2.5.head: نال
36.2.5.meaning: A lavish giver, addressed by a name made from the word for bounty.

37.2.5.head: اِحتالَ
37.2.5.meaning: To devise a skilful means of achieving an end.

39.2.4.head: تِنبال
39.2.4.meaning: A short man, here representing narrowness of character or standing.

40.2.4.head: قَدر
40.2.4.meaning: Men’s degrees of honour. His rank can walk proudly among other ranks even when the man himself declines to strut.

41.2.4.head: مِفضال
41.2.4.meaning: Someone habitually lavish in doing others good.

42.1.4.head: مُهجَة
42.1.4.meaning: The heart’s blood, hence life itself.

42.2.5.head: رَوع
42.2.5.meaning: The fear of an encounter, especially in battle.

45.2.5.head: إِجمال
45.2.5.meaning: Decent treatment or gracious conduct. People earn the word here just by refraining from doing something ugly.

46.2.2.head: قاتَ
46.2.2.meaning: Sustained him with the food he needed.

46.2.3-4.head: فُضول العَيش
46.2.3-4.meaning: “The surplus of living”, whatever exceeds the necessities of life.
